questions.q: What is the core trade-off this lesson describes between GUI diagramming tools and diagram-as-code tools?
options: GUI tools offer fast visual manipulation and polish; diagram-as-code tools trade some visual polish for text-based version control and diffability
GUI tools are always free; diagram-as-code tools always cost money
There is no real trade-off — the two tool families are functionally identical
Diagram-as-code tools can only produce ERDs, never sequence diagrams
questions.explain: GUI tools (Lucidchart, diagrams.net, Visio) are strong for fast, polished visual layout; diagram-as-code tools (Mermaid, PlantUML) represent diagrams as text, gaining version control and diffability at some cost to visual polish and layout control.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a diagram-as-code file solves a problem GUI-tool files generally don't?
options: Because diagram-as-code files render faster in a browser
Because a text-based diagram file can be stored in Git, reviewed in a pull request, and diffed line by line, while a binary GUI-tool file just shows 'the image changed' with no visible internal diff
Because GUI tools cannot export to PNG or SVG
Because diagram-as-code tools do not require any syntax to learn
questions.explain: Diagram-as-code's key advantage is diffability: a text file versions cleanly alongside code in Git with a visible line-by-line diff, which a proprietary binary diagram file can't offer.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is Schema Builder's role relative to producing final architecture documentation?
options: It is the complete, final documentation artifact and needs no further work
It cannot display any custom object relationships

It's useful for live exploration of the org's current metadata and can be a starting point (especially with a third-party export extension), but it isn't built to produce a durable, annotated, version-stamped documentation artifact on its own
It replaces the need for a legend entirely
questions.explain: Schema Builder draws a live, metadata-accurate view and can be a reasonable starting point (via export), but per Lesson 8's standards, a real documentation artifact still needs annotation, a legend, and a version stamp added afterward.

questions.q: According to the lesson's tool-selection table, which kind of tool is the more reasonable choice when a diagram must version alongside a Salesforce DX project's code in Git?
options: A cloud GUI tool chosen purely for its template library
Microsoft Visio, because of its Microsoft 365 integration
Schema Builder's native export only
Diagram-as-code tools like Mermaid or PlantUML, because of their text-based diffability
questions.explain: The lesson's table specifically recommends diagram-as-code tools for diagrams that must version alongside a DX project's code, since their text format diffs cleanly in Git.

questions.q: What does this lesson conclude about choosing 'the correct' diagramming tool for a Solution Design Document?
options: No single tool is correct for every document; what matters is that whichever tool is used, the result still follows the documentation set's agreed notation standard from Lesson 8
There is one tool every Salesforce architect is required to use for all diagrams
GUI tools should never be used for official documentation
Diagram-as-code tools should never be used for executive-facing diagrams
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly concludes that tool choice depends on the need (speed/polish vs. version control vs. metadata accuracy), but every diagram, regardless of tool, still needs to follow the set's agreed notation standard.
